properties.Session: EAPC Groups: Palliative oxygen therapy: preliminary guidelines and reconsideration within the palliative care continuum
properties.Chairs: Prof Sabina Antoniu, Prof Magnus Ekström, Dr Slavica Kochovska, Dr Filip Bjorklund

content:
This session is planned to discuss clinical guidelines regarding palliative oxygen therapy. These guidelines are generated by the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Oxygen Therapy and regard POT definition, outcome measures follow up and regimens. This task force was developed in recognition of the need to support the use of palliative oxygen therapy. Currently, its use is limited due to a lack of a consensual definition, due to unclear eligibility, limited evidence supporting various regimens (low flow versus high flow therapy) and the lack of validated outcome measures. We established several working groups within this Task Force and tried to gather and analyse the existing evidence on the above mentioned issues. Some of the evidence is generated via systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature, and some other is generated based on consensus elicited via the Delphi procedure. For both categories, it would be very useful to have an interactive exchange of opinions before wrapping everything up and drafting the clinical guideline paper.

Questions and learning objectives:  
How should palliative oxygen therapy be defined? 
Should low-flow oxygen therapy be used to improve symptoms in people with chronic serious illness who do not meet the criteria for LTOT? 
Should high-flow oxygen therapy be used to improve symptoms in people with chronic serious illness who do not meet the criteria for LTOT? 
What are the eligibility criteria for palliative oxygen therapy? 
How should palliative oxygen therapy be administered and followed up? 

Speakers:

Prof Sabina Antoniu, University of Medicine and Pharmacy Grigore T Popa Iasi, Romania 
Prof Magnus Ekström, Lund University, Sweden

Dr Slavica Kochovska, Flinders University Adelaide, Australia
Dr Filip Bjorklund, Lund University, Sweden

All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Oxygen Therapy.

properties.Session: TS: Methodological approaches to research into requests for assisted dying: added value & challenges
properties.Chairs: Prof Mette Asbjoern Neergaard, None Guillaume Economos

content:
Research into Requests for Assisted Dying.

In this themed session, participants will engage with diverse research on requests for assisted dying in palliative care, conducted using distinct methodologies and situated in different countries and contexts. The main emphasis will be on the employed methodologies, examining the novelty and added value of each approach in uncovering relevant insights, as well as the challenges and pitfalls they present in data collection and analysis. Through a rich and in-depth group interaction process, participants will leave the session with a range of recommendations for further research and practice.

Content of the session:- Short introduction to the session
- Three concise presentations on research into requests for assisted dying, which, next to sharing the main findings, will focus on the methodologies used, their added value, and the complexities encountered. Each contribution will centre on a distinct methodological approach:
1) international comparative research;
2) qualitative ethnographic approaches;
3) consensus-building methods
- a moderated group discussion on issues related to doing research on assisted dying (and its relationship to palliative care).

content:
Panel 3: Issues with implementation
This panel will explore barriers such as regulatory variation, workforce capacity, cultural differences, integration into routine care, sustainability beyond project funding, and uneven adoption across countries. The session will identify practical strategies from implementation science to enhance scalability, long-term impact, and real-world uptake of palliative care innovations across Europe.
Panellists: Elias Lundereng (MyPath), Lieve van den Block (EuNavigate), Sergi Navaro (PALLIAKID), Suzanne Timmons (IN TOUCH and AI4Hope)
Panel 4: Moving research into practice
This panel will examine the gap between evidence generation and real-world adoption, exploring knowledge translation strategies, stakeholder engagement and sustainable service integration across diverse European health systems. The session will highlight practical models and success factors that enable research findings to influence clinical practice and organisational change at scale.
Panellists: Katrine Rolid (EUonQOL, JANE2), Roman Rolke (RAPHAEL), Ulf Bremberg (PsyPal)

properties.Session: EAPC Groups: Palliative Care Meets Emergency Medical Services. An International Call to Action
properties.Chairs: Dr Caleb Gage, Dr Eva Diehl-Wiesenecker, Dr Madeleine Juhrmann, Dr Martin Loučka

content:
The integration of palliative care into out-of-hospital emergency services is gaining momentum worldwide. People with life-limiting illnesses often face acute medical emergencies, which, in the absence of clear communication and structural pathways, may lead to distressing overtreatment from emergency care workers. This session presents experiences from South Africa, Australia and Germany on systematically strengthening palliative care within EMS — from provider and patient surveys to concrete implementation concepts, in addition to an overview of the state of palliative paramedicine affairs globally. Building on these insights, a proposal for a European White Paper will be introduced. The session aims to foster international exchange and develop joint recommendations for improving palliative care in EMS across Europe and further abroad.

The aims and learning objectives:

 - Understand the unique role of Emergency Medical Services (EMS) in delivering palliative care.  
 - Explore how integrating palliative care benefits EMS, palliative care services, patient outcomes and the broader healthcare system, through a global systems lens. 
 - Learn from international models, including South Africa (low-to-middle income country context), Australia and Germany.  
 - Identify key elements for implementation such as communication, documentation, education and policy. 
 - Reflect on how these insights can inform local practice and support a European framework.

Speakers:

Dr Caleb Gage, Paramedic, University of Cape Town, South Africa, 
Dr Eva Diehl-Wiesenecker, Consultant Emergency Medicine, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany; Department of Palliative Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, University of Augsburg, Germany
Dr Madeleine Juhrmann. Post-Doctoral Research Fellow, University of New South Wales, Australia
Dr Martin Loucka, Founder, Center for Palliative Care, Czech Republic

All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Care & Emergency Medical Services

content:
Session One. 
Wordcraft: Optimising writing for publication
This session will consist of two main elements: 
1.          All the World’s a Stage: Academic Writing for an International Audience
2.          Mad About Methods: Writing a Well-Crafted Methods SectionAim: To equip participants with some of the skills and knowledge needed to successfully publish research in palliative care journals. 
Learning objectives:

 Learning how to write for a global audience by using clear,      accessible language and framing research in a broadly relevant context;
 Developing the ability to construct transparent and rigorous      methods and ethics sections aligned with reporting standards.

By the end of this interactive session, participants will be better prepared to navigate the publication process and enhance the clarity, credibility, and impact of their palliative care research.
This session brings together three editors from the EAPC journals: Catherine Walshe and Sandra Martins Pereira from Palliative Medicine, and Christopher Jones from the Journal of Palliative Medicine. Together, they will share all you ever wanted to know about how to get your work published. Two interlinked and interactive sessions (this session today, and a second session tomorrow)  will focus on some of the most important aspects to ensure your work goes out for peer review (writing for your international audience and persuading the reader of the robustness of your methods and ethics procedures), and then, tomorrow,  how to respond appropriately to the peer review comments. If you have ever wanted to really understand how editors make their decisions on your research papers – these are the sessions for you.
